reply.recognition: Recognized from supplied metadata as UCI Appliances Energy Prediction (UCI 374), associated with Candanedo et al. (2017), Data driven prediction models of energy use of appliances in a low-energy house. No remembered result is presented as new.
reply.summary: Propose a testable monitoring idea for one-household energy use beyond another aggregate predictor. Evidence: 19,735 ten-minute observations from one house over about 4.5 months; aggregate Appliances and lights energy, room temperature/humidity sensors, north-side outdoor T6/RH_6, partly interpolated airport weather, and documented random features rv1/rv2. The proposed increment tests whether delayed zone-specific thermal response adds an operational signal to aggregate energy monitoring. It cannot identify occupancy, appliance switching, or causal effects.

candidates.title: Thermal after-response as a monitor for sustained high household appliance load
candidates.question: After a high Appliances energy interval, is there a delayed increase in laundry and ironing zone temperature beyond matched low-load periods with similar clock time, pre-event temperatures, and outdoor temperature change?
candidates.new_claim: Input-level increment: test a preregistered lagged thermal-response contrast as a monitoring signal for sustained high aggregate appliance-energy episodes, rather than predicting the same-interval aggregate target. This is a hypothesis about observability, not device or occupant attribution or a literature novelty claim.
candidates.input_delta: The task frames the data as regression and describes room sensors, ten-minute aggregation, and aggregate Appliances energy. The proposed addition links high-load episodes to a future 30-60 minute zone-temperature response and monitoring use. T3 is the laundry room and T7 the ironing room per supplied variable information.
candidates.domain_value: If prospectively validated, a delayed zone response could flag sustained energy episodes for review and prioritize where to add submeters. It cannot identify a device or justify automated control by itself.
known_basis_refs: materials.official_documentation.variables: Appliances and lights are separately measured energy in Wh; T3 is laundry-room temperature; T7 is ironing-room temperature.

materials.official_documentation.additional_info: energy is logged every ten minutes; wireless temperature/humidity readings are averaged over ten-minute periods; two random variables were included for regression testing.
materials.case.unit: one house, about 4.5 months; outdoor weather is partly interpolated; occupancy/appliance-level switching is not directly measured.
materials.data_profile: 19,735 rows; Appliances quantiles are supplied at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0 only (median 60 Wh, maximum 1,080 Wh); no 90th percentile is assumed.
assumptions: A portion of some sustained electrical loads may produce detectable room heat, but fraction and location are unknown.
High aggregate Appliances energy can include heterogeneous devices and cannot be equated with one appliance or activity.
Clock time, pre-event thermal state, and observed weather suffice for an initial observational contrast; residual confounding and interpolation error remain.
Rows are serially dependent; day-level or longer blocks, not individual rows, must govern uncertainty.

variables_and_units.exposure: Appliances, Wh per ten-minute interval; define high-load threshold before inspecting post-event temperatures and specify event merging.
variables_and_units.separate_load: lights, Wh per ten-minute interval; retain or match because it is separately measured.
variables_and_units.primary_outcome: Mean of T3 and T7 temperature change in degrees C from the pre-event 30-minute mean to the 30-60 minute post-event mean.
variables_and_units.covariates: T_out in degrees C (airport-derived, partly interpolated), T6 in degrees C (north-side outdoor sensor), pre-event T3/T7 in degrees C, clock time, and day of week.
variables_and_units.placebo: Same temperature contrast over the 30-60 minutes before the high-load event.
variables_and_units.independent_unit: One household time series; use contiguous day-level or longer blocks for uncertainty, not row-wise independence.

candidates.testable_prediction: Compared with low-load controls matched on clock time, pre-event T3/T7, and observed outdoor conditions, high-load events will have a positive mean 30-60 minute post-event T3/T7 temperature-change contrast, with a day-block confidence interval excluding zero. The corresponding pre-event lead contrast should be near zero. Freeze direction and window before computation.
candidates.alternative: The apparent response reflects weather or time-of-day structure, reverse timing, sensor averaging, interpolation, or selection of unusual periods; alternatively, heterogeneous load location and heat output leave no stable thermal signature.
candidates.discriminating_test: Run a matched event study with day-block uncertainty. Compare the predeclared post-event contrast with the pre-event lead placebo and matched low-load exposure. Report independent event days and sensitivity to high-load threshold. A prospective follow-up should log room-level plug/submeter Wh and device activity to test the monitoring interpretation.
candidates.feasible_with_current_data: The broker has the complete timestamped dataframe and required energy and sensor columns, so observational lag and placebo contrasts are computable. Results establish only a single-house association, not device attribution, causal heating, or generalization.
candidates.required_new_data: For monitoring validation, collect synchronized room-level plug/submeter Wh, appliance on/off labels, and room temperature at ten-minute or finer resolution in multiple homes. Record occupancy only if activity attribution is intended. Compare high-load episodes with matched low-load periods and predeclare alert precision or sensitivity/specificity.
candidates.failure_condition: Withdraw the thermal-monitoring signal if the post-event contrast is non-positive or its day-block interval includes zero, if the pre-event lead is comparably positive, or if the signal is not robust to reasonable event-threshold and weather-matching choices.
candidates.nearest_prior_query: Crossref query to test proximity: residential appliance energy event detection using indoor temperature sensors, lagged thermal response, and submeter ground truth. The supplied 2017 paper concerns data-driven prediction of appliance energy; its uninspected full text is not used to claim novelty.

candidates.title: Zone-specific thermal coupling as an operational ventilation-change monitor
candidates.question: Do zone-specific lags between north-side outdoor T6 and indoor temperatures T1-T9 reveal periods of increased indoor-outdoor thermal coupling that merit ventilation or envelope inspection?
candidates.new_claim: Input-level increment: evaluate a change-point monitor based on zone response lag to measured north-side outdoor temperature, then validate whether it corresponds to window/ventilation state. This proposal does not claim the data measure window opening or building heat loss.
candidates.input_delta: The data include indoor temperatures by named room, T6 measured outside on the north side, and airport T_out with some interpolation. The proposed target is a changing zone-specific response lag, not aggregate energy prediction.
candidates.domain_value: A validated flag could direct an energy team to inspect unusual ventilation or envelope conditions before interpreting consumption changes as occupant behavior.
known_basis_refs: materials.official_documentation.variables: T1-T9 are room-specific temperatures; T6 is outside on the north side; T_out is airport weather.
materials.official_documentation.additional_info: room temperature/humidity observations were averaged over ten-minute periods; hourly airport weather was interpolated.
materials.case.unit: single house with no direct occupancy or appliance-switching measurement.
assumptions: T6 and indoor sensors are sufficiently synchronized to estimate lag at ten-minute resolution.
Rapid zone response can arise from ventilation or envelope coupling, but solar gains, internal heat, sensor placement, and other causes are alternatives.
Enough independent outdoor-temperature transitions exist to assess feasibility; unknown until computation.

variables_and_units.input: T6 and T_out, degrees C at ten-minute intervals.
variables_and_units.response: T1-T9, degrees C at ten-minute intervals.
variables_and_units.diagnostic: Zone-specific lag or response coefficient with a defined estimation window and uncertainty.
variables_and_units.validation_target: Window/ventilation state and HVAC state, measured prospectively; neither is supplied.

candidates.testable_prediction: If useful, candidate periods with shorter T6-to-indoor response lag in one zone will be associated with independently logged window/ventilation changes there, compared with matched periods without such changes.
candidates.alternative: Lag shifts reflect seasonal drift, airport interpolation, indoor gains, sensor placement, or autocorrelation rather than ventilation or envelope state.
candidates.discriminating_test: Assess lag stability in blocked time segments using available sensors, then prospectively compare flagged and unflagged ten-minute windows against window contacts and HVAC logs, with sensitivity and false-alert rate fixed in advance.
candidates.feasible_with_current_data: Descriptive lag stability is testable; identifying ventilation events or diagnostic accuracy is impossible without state labels.
candidates.required_new_data: Window-contact and HVAC on/off logs, plus repeated measurements in several homes and zones, synchronized with T6, T_out, and T1-T9.
candidates.failure_condition: Reject the monitor if estimated lag shifts are not reproducible across blocked periods or do not predict logged state changes above a prespecified baseline alert rate.
candidates.nearest_prior_query: Crossref query to test proximity: residential window opening detection from indoor-outdoor temperature time series and zone thermal response.

candidates.title: Persistent overnight appliance energy as a standby-load audit trigger
candidates.question: Does aggregate Appliances energy persist overnight when lights are zero and measured room temperatures are stable, enough to justify a plug-level standby-load audit?
candidates.new_claim: Input-level increment: turn recurring low-activity overnight consumption into a defined audit trigger, separating an operational screening rule from an unsupported claim that the energy is standby consumption.
candidates.input_delta: The task identifies separately measured Appliances and lights energy at ten-minute cadence. The proposed use detects recurring overnight energy persistence and triggers submeters rather than fitting another aggregate predictor.
candidates.domain_value: A screening rule could prioritize homes or periods for plug-level auditing and potential standby-load reduction.
known_basis_refs: materials.official_documentation.variables: Appliances and lights are separate energy variables in Wh.
materials.official_documentation.additional_info: energy is logged at ten-minute intervals.
materials.data_profile: Appliances has supplied median 60 Wh; overnight-specific summaries are not supplied.
assumptions: Clock time defines an overnight window, but lights=0 and stable temperatures do not prove occupant absence or lack of active devices.
A persistent aggregate floor could include refrigeration, heating, or necessary loads and cannot be called standby without device measurements.

variables_and_units.energy: Appliances and lights, Wh per ten-minute interval.
variables_and_units.context: Timestamp and T1-T9, degrees C, used for a prespecified stable-temperature condition.
variables_and_units.audit_unit: Contiguous overnight episode and household, not independent ten-minute rows.

candidates.testable_prediction: A subset of overnight blocks with lights=0 and stable room temperatures will show recurring Appliances energy above the low-load floor on multiple nights; plug-level follow-up should identify a measurable, controllable portion.
candidates.alternative: Energy is necessary refrigeration/heating or unmeasured occupant/device use; the screening condition may not predict controllable standby energy.
candidates.discriminating_test: Estimate recurrence of the defined overnight condition in the current series, then instrument circuits with plug-level submeters for at least two weeks. Compare flagged and matched unflagged nights and quantify controllable Wh/day.
candidates.feasible_with_current_data: Recurrence of aggregate overnight patterns is computable, but occupancy absence and standby-device attribution are unobserved.
candidates.required_new_data: Plug-level Wh by device or circuit, occupancy/activity diary or sensor if making absence claims, and repeated nights across households.
candidates.failure_condition: Do not use the screen for standby-load interventions if flagged periods lack a reproducible controllable plug-level load above matched unflagged baseline.
candidates.nearest_prior_query: Crossref query to test proximity: residential standby energy detection from smart meter load profiles, night baseload screening, and plug-level validation.

task.deliverable: Critique I1 and return a preregisterable event-study specification plus one computation request and one focused Crossref search request if useful. Estimate the predeclared 30-60 minute T3/T7 post-event contrast for high Appliances-energy episodes against low-load controls matched on clock time, pre-event thermal state, and observed outdoor conditions; quantify uncertainty with day-level or longer contiguous blocks; report the corresponding pre-event lead placebo. Do not report row-wise p-values as independent evidence or infer causal/device-specific effects. State event threshold, de-duplication, matching, missing/edge handling, and sensitivity checks before reading results. Search prior residential energy-event and indoor-temperature-sensor work.
acceptance: Keep or revise the frozen prediction explicitly, and provide a plausible alternative and a result that would falsify the monitoring signal.
Return complete executable analysis code only if requesting computation; it must use DF, avoid I/O, print compact valid JSON, and run within broker limits.
Use the same time ordering and event/control definitions for the post-event contrast and lead placebo; account for serial dependence with day-level or longer blocks.
Separate an observational lag association from causal claims, occupancy inference, appliance identification, or cross-home generalization.
If searching, use one Crossref query about the lagged thermal-response monitoring relation and report only what returned source metadata supports.
task.proposed_computation: Request a blocked event study on the complete supplied DF. Freeze high-load event thresholding and episode merging before inspecting outcomes; compare T3/T7 mean temperature change from the pre-event 30-minute baseline to the 30-60 minute post-event window against controls matched on clock time, pre-event temperatures, and T_out/T6. Report contrast in degrees C, day-block uncertainty, event/event-day counts, identically defined pre-event lead placebo, and sensitivity to threshold and matching. No results exist in this L1 turn.
task.proposed_search: Crossref query: residential appliance energy event monitoring using lagged indoor room temperature response, with submeter or appliance-state validation; compare thermal-signature monitoring to aggregate energy prediction.
